newsitem.title: UK: LME nickel rockets higher, more gains seen.
newsitem.headline: LME nickel rockets higher, more gains seen.

text.p: LME nickel steamed higher on Monday afternoon on mainly chart buying and short-covering, but the other metals held to narrow ranges.
Three months nickel peaked at $6,945 per tonne, a gain of $340 or five percent on Friday's afternoon kerb close, after it earlier broke above a key trendline, analysts said.
"Once it broke above the nearby downtrend line at $6,637 we saw some very good technical buying and short covering," said analyst William Adams of broker Rudolf Wolff.
"But I don't think we've seen the bulk of the short-covering yet," he added.
Nickel had become oversold recently as funds went short, bottoming at $6,365 on December 30.
Last year, prices hit a high of $8,850 in February.
Fundamentals have been bleak with sluggish demand from the stainless steel sector, which accounts for two thirds of Western world nickel consumption.
But stainless steel output is expected to grow in 1997, with some analysts seeing an increase of five percent.
Technically, resistance is pegged at $6,950, then $7,090.
By the end of the kerb, profit-taking had taken the froth off the market to end at $6,860, up $255.
The other metals marked time, holding in tight price bands.
Copper finished $2 higher at $2,195, after turning back from resistance at $2,200 ahead of stocks data on Tuesday, which some traders are expecting to show an increase.
On Friday, inventories fell by 2,125 tonnes.
"If stocks fall again, I think you could see prices make it through $2,215 resistance," Adams said.
Aluminium finished the day at $1,552, down $2.
Analysts say the market needs to consolidate further before tackling solid resistance at $1,570, where producer selling is expected to make progress difficult.
Support was pegged at $1,530.
Zinc ended at $1,064, up $2 and lead closed $4 weaker at $696.
Tin finished the kerb unchanged at $5,760 while aluminium alloy was indicated at $1,430/35, little changed from Friday's $1,430/33.
--Eric Onstad, London Newsroom +44 171 542 8065
